title: The Secure Shell (SSH) Protocol Architecture
subtitle: The blueprint for logging in to a distant machine without letting anyone on the wire listen in.
summary: RFC 4251 describes the overall design of the Secure Shell (SSH) protocol: a transport layer that authenticates the server and encrypts the connection, a user authentication layer that proves who the client is, and a connection layer that carries many channels over one tunnel. It also defines the data types, the algorithm naming scheme and the message number ranges shared by the other SSH documents, and gathers the security considerations for the whole family.

eli5.summary: SSH is like a locked, soundproof tube between your computer and a faraway one. First you check that you are at the right door, then you show who you are, and then you can send as many notes through the tube as you like.

tldr.problem: Remote login tools such as telnet and rlogin sent passwords and data in clear text over networks anyone could watch.
tldr.mechanism: SSH stacks three protocols: a transport layer that authenticates the server host key and encrypts and integrity-protects the stream, a user authentication layer, and a connection layer that multiplexes channels such as shells and port forwards.
tldr.outcome: It became the standard way to administer remote machines securely, and this document is the shared foundation that the transport, authentication, connection and numbers documents build on.

today: SSH is the everyday tool for remote administration of servers, network equipment and cloud machines, and it also carries file transfer (SFTP, SCP) and Git over SSH. OpenSSH is the most widely deployed implementation. Several algorithms mentioned in this 2006 text, such as the required DSS public key algorithm, 3DES and the diffie-hellman-group1-sha1 key exchange, are now considered weak or deprecated, and RFC 8308 later updated the architecture with a way to negotiate extensions, but the three-layer design and the naming scheme remain in use.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Secure Shell (SSH) is a protocol for secure remote login and other secure network services over an insecure network. This document is the architecture overview of a set of documents; it does not itself define the byte-by-byte exchange. Instead it describes how the pieces fit together and defines the vocabulary the others share.

The RFC names three major components, each running on top of the one before it:

Transport Layer Protocol
Provides server authentication, confidentiality and integrity, and may optionally provide compression. It will typically run over a TCP/IP connection but could use any reliable data stream.
User Authentication Protocol
Authenticates the client-side user to the server, running over the transport layer.
Connection Protocol
Multiplexes the encrypted tunnel into several logical channels, running over the user authentication protocol.

The client sends a service request once a secure transport connection exists, and a second one after user authentication is complete. That lets new protocols be defined and coexist with the ones above. The details live in RFC 4252 (authentication), RFC 4253 (transport) and RFC 4254 (connection), with IANA registries described in RFC 4250.
sections.eli5: Think of mailing a secret message through a busy post office. First you make sure you are really talking to the right mail clerk and agree on a secret code. Then you show your ID. Only after that can you send as many different letters as you want. SSH does those three things in that order.

sections.title: The Three-Layer Architecture
sections.content:
Each layer relies on the guarantees of the layer beneath it. The transport protocol performs server host authentication, key exchange, encryption and integrity protection, and it derives a unique session id that higher-level protocols may use. The authentication protocol then uses that session id and the transport's protection to check who the user is. The connection protocol finally gives the authenticated user useful things to do.

The connection protocol provides channels that can be used for a wide range of purposes. Standard methods are provided for setting up secure interactive shell sessions and for forwarding ("tunneling") arbitrary TCP/IP ports and X11 connections.

Because services are requested by name after each layer is established, new protocols can be defined later without changing the transport. This is how SSH grew from a remote shell into a general secure tunnel.

The protocol also allows full negotiation of encryption, integrity, key exchange, compression and public key algorithms and formats. Encryption, integrity, public key and compression algorithms can be different for each direction. The RFC lists policy issues each implementation should expose in its configuration, including the preferred algorithm in each category, which authentication methods the server requires for each user, and what the user may do through the connection protocol. For example, policy SHOULD NOT allow the server to start sessions or run commands on the client machine.
sections.eli5: The tube has three floors. The ground floor makes the tube private. The middle floor checks your ID. The top floor lets you open lots of little doors, one for a chat window, one for a file, and so on, all inside the same tube.

sections.title: Host Keys and Trust
sections.content:
Each server host SHOULD have a host key, and may have several using different algorithms. The host key is used during key exchange to verify that the client is really talking to the correct server. For that to work, the client must have a priori knowledge of the server's public host key. The RFC describes two trust models.

  • The client keeps a local database that associates each host name with the corresponding public host key. This needs no central infrastructure, but the database may become burdensome to maintain.
  • A trusted certification authority (CA) certifies the host name-to-key association, so the client only needs the CA root key. This eases maintenance but places a lot of trust in the central infrastructure.

The protocol also allows the name-to-key association not to be checked on the first connection. That still protects against passive listening, but leaves the connection open to active man-in-the-middle attacks, so implementations SHOULD NOT normally allow it by default. The RFC suggests a pragmatic strategy: accept an unchecked key the first time, save it in a local database, and compare against it on every later connection.

The working group argued that ease of use is critical to acceptance, and that no security is gained if the new solution is not used. That is why the unchecked first-connection option exists, even though it reduces security where it is allowed.

Implementations MAY also show a fingerprint derived from a SHA-1 hash of the public key, which can be verified by telephone or another outside channel.
sections.eli5: Each computer has a special stamp that nobody else can copy. The first time you visit, you write down what its stamp looks like. Next time, if the stamp looks different, you get a warning that somebody might be pretending to be your friend.

sections.title: Naming and Extensibility
sections.content:
The designers expected the protocol to evolve and organizations to want their own encryption, authentication or key exchange methods. Central registration of everything is cumbersome, but no registration at all leads to conflicting identifiers. The compromise is that algorithms, methods and formats are identified by textual names of a specific format, and DNS names are used to create local namespaces.

All algorithm and method identifiers MUST be printable US-ASCII, non-empty strings no longer than 64 characters, and names are case-sensitive. There are two formats:

Names without an at-sign
Reserved for assignment by IETF CONSENSUS and valid only once registered with the IANA. Examples include "3des-cbc", "sha-1", "hmac-sha1" and "zlib".
name@domainname
Anyone can define their own, such as "ourcipher-cbc@example.com". The part after the at-sign MUST be a fully qualified domain name controlled by the person or organization defining the name.

The base protocol is kept as simple as possible, but all implementations MUST support a minimal set of mandatory algorithms to ensure interoperability, even if local policy does not allow them. Those algorithms are specified in the transport, authentication and connection documents.
sections.eli5: Everyone can use the official list of names, like names in a school roll book. If you want to invent your own, you put your own address after the at-sign, like writing your name and street on your own toy so it can never be mixed up with someone else's.

sections.title: Data Type Representations
sections.content:
All SSH messages are built from a small set of data types, defined here once so the other documents can refer to them. Fields are written in a message definition as a type and a name, for example SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_DATA is a byte, a uint32 recipient channel and a string data field.

  • byte: an arbitrary 8-bit value (octet).
  • boolean: one byte, 0 for FALSE and 1 for TRUE. All non-zero values MUST be interpreted as TRUE, but applications MUST NOT store values other than 0 and 1.
  • uint32: a 32-bit unsigned integer in network byte order. The value 699921578 (0x29b7f4aa) is stored as 29 b7 f4 aa.
  • uint64: a 64-bit unsigned integer in network byte order.
  • string: arbitrary binary data stored as a uint32 length followed by that many bytes, with no terminating null. The string "testing" is 00 00 00 07 t e s t i n g.
  • mpint: a multiple precision integer in two's complement, stored as a string, most significant byte first. The value zero is a string with zero bytes of data, and -1234 is 00 00 00 02 ed cc.
  • name-list: a string containing a comma-separated list of names, each non-empty and without a comma, in US-ASCII.

Text is US-ASCII for internal names and ISO 10646 UTF-8 for anything that might be shown to a user, such as user names.
sections.eli5: Computers need to agree on how to write numbers and words as boxes of bytes. SSH says: always write how long a thing is first, and then write the thing. It is like putting a label saying "4 letters" on a bag before the letters go in.

sections.title: Message Numbers and IANA
sections.content:
SSH packets have message numbers in the range 1 to 255. This document divides that space so that each layer, and each kind of message within a layer, has its own block. Method-specific ranges can be reused for different key exchange or authentication methods, because only one method is in use at a time.

Names without an at-sign in the categories the RFC lists (service names, authentication methods, connection protocol channel and request names, key exchange method names, and encryption, MAC, public key and compression algorithm names) are assigned by IETF consensus. Each category has its own namespace, but using the same name in several categories SHOULD be avoided. Message numbers 0 to 191 are allocated by IETF CONSENSUS, and 192 to 255 (local extensions) are reserved for PRIVATE USE.

The binding instructions to the IANA are in RFC 4250, not here; this section is only a convenience summary and says so itself.
sections.eli5: Every kind of SSH message gets a number, like page numbers in a book. The book has chapters: numbers 1 to 49 for building the tube, 50 to 79 for showing ID, 80 to 127 for the doors and channels, and the pages from 192 on are left blank for your own notes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security discussion for the whole SSH family is gathered here. The transport protocol gives a confidential channel with host authentication, key exchange, encryption and integrity protection. Highlights include:

  • Random numbers. Session keys are bound to the session by random data, so the generator must be cryptographically secure with proper entropy. If entropy is short, refusing to run the protocol is preferable to using weak random numbers.
  • The "none" options. The "none" cipher and "none" MAC exist for debugging and SHOULD NOT be used otherwise.
  • CBC attack. The Rogaway attack on CBC mode can be mitigated by sending SSH_MSG_IGNORE packets so the attacker cannot predict the next initialization vector.
  • Rekeying. Because MACs use a 32-bit sequence number, the transport protocol recommends rekeying after one gigabyte of data, and with a smallest packet of 16 bytes this means rekeying SHOULD happen after 2**28 packets at the very most.
  • Man-in-the-middle. Using SSH without a reliable association between a host and its host key is inherently insecure and is NOT RECOMMENDED, though it still protects against passive attacks.
  • Forward secrecy. Diffie-Hellman key exchanges may provide perfect forward secrecy, and by the RFC's definition SSH does have it, though that property is not passed on to protocols running over SSH.
  • Denial of service and traffic analysis. An attacker can force expensive key exchange work, and traffic analysis has been shown to reveal the length of a password; random padding and SSH_MSG_IGNORE help.

Authentication is no stronger than the weakest combination of methods the server allows. Password authentication assumes the server is not compromised, public key authentication assumes the client is not, and host-based authentication assumes the client has not been compromised. Forwarding through the connection protocol may also let users bypass site firewall policy.
sections.eli5: A tube is only as safe as the rules around it. Use strong locks, never leave the lock turned off, check who is at the other end, and do not let people sneak extra doors through your fence without asking.
